claim: IRE1 is conserved in all eukaryotes.
source: IRE1, conserved in all eukaryotes and therefore the best-studied UPR transducer (Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993), detects ER stress via its luminal domain (IRE1LD), initiating dimerisation-dependent autophosphorylation of its cytosolic domain (Shamu and Walter, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cox et al., 1993 and Mori et al., 1993

claim: IRE1 detects ER stress via its luminal domain (IRE1LD).
source: IRE1, conserved in all eukaryotes and therefore the best-studied UPR transducer (Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993), detects ER stress via its luminal domain (IRE1LD), initiating dimerisation-dependent autophosphorylation of its cytosolic domain (Shamu and Walter, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shamu and Walter, 1996

claim: IRE1 activation initiates dimerisation-dependent autophosphorylation of its cytosolic domain.
source: IRE1, conserved in all eukaryotes and therefore the best-studied UPR transducer (Cox et al., 1993; Mori et al., 1993), detects ER stress via its luminal domain (IRE1LD), initiating dimerisation-dependent autophosphorylation of its cytosolic domain (Shamu and Walter, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shamu and Walter, 1996

claim: Autophosphorylation of IRE1's cytosolic domain leads to allosteric activation of the cytosolic endoribonuclease domain.
source: The subsequent allosteric activation of the cytosolic endoribonuclease domain (Lee et al., 2008) leads to unconventional splicing of the mRNA encoding the XBP1/HAC1 transcription factor (Cox and Walter, 1996; Yoshida et al., 2001; Calfon et al., 2002), thereby promoting translation of an effector that drives a conserved gene-expression program.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008

claim: IRE1 endoribonuclease activity leads to unconventional splicing of the mRNA encoding the XBP1/HAC1 transcription factor.
source: The subsequent allosteric activation of the cytosolic endoribonuclease domain (Lee et al., 2008) leads to unconventional splicing of the mRNA encoding the XBP1/HAC1 transcription factor (Cox and Walter, 1996; Yoshida et al., 2001; Calfon et al., 2002), thereby promoting translation of an effector that drives a conserved gene-expression program.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cox and Walter, 1996; Yoshida et al., 2001; Calfon et al., 2002

claim: The crystal structure of the core luminal domain from S. cerevisiae IRE1 shows an IRE1LD dimer interface traversed by a groove with architectural similarity to MHC peptide-binding complexes.
source: This model is supported by the crystal structure of the core luminal domain from S. cerevisae IRE1, showing an IRE1LD dimer interface traversed by a groove with architectural similarity to the major histocompatibility peptide-binding complexes (MHCs) (Credle et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Credle et al., 2005

claim: Peptide ligands of yeast IRE1LD have been identified and their addition enhances the population of higher order species.
source: Peptide ligands of the yeast IRE1LD have been identified and their addition to dilute solutions of yeast IRE1LD enhances the population of higher order species, although a clear shift from monomers to dimers was not readily observable (Gardner and Walter, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gardner and Walter, 2011

claim: The luminal domain of human IRE1α crystallises as a dimer with overall architecture similar to the yeast protein.
source: The luminal domain of the broadly expressed alpha isoform of human IRE1 (hIRE1αLD) also crystallises as a dimer, with an overall architecture similar to the yeast protein, however, barring conformational changes, the MHC-like groove is too narrow to accommodate a peptide (Zhou et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2006

claim: The MHC-like groove in human IRE1αLD is too narrow to accommodate a peptide.
source: The luminal domain of the broadly expressed alpha isoform of human IRE1 (hIRE1αLD) also crystallises as a dimer, with an overall architecture similar to the yeast protein, however, barring conformational changes, the MHC-like groove is too narrow to accommodate a peptide (Zhou et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2006

claim: Peptides have been identified that bind hIRE1LD and affect its oligomeric state as assessed by analytical ultracentrifugation.
source: Recently, peptides have been identified that bind hIRE1LD and affect its oligomeric state, as assessed by analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC). Moreover, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) reported on peptide-induced structural rearrangements within the hIRE1αLD that also affected residues near the MHC-like groove. Hence, it has been proposed that the structure of Zhou et al. (2006) represents a 'closed' conformation of the peptide-binding groove that can shift towards an 'open' state to allow peptide binding (Karagöz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karagöz et al., 2017

claim: There is an inverse correlation between ER stress-induced IRE1 activity and the amount of ER-localised BiP recovered in complex with it.
source: This model is supported by an inverse correlation between ER stress-induced IRE1 activity and the amount of ER-localised BiP recovered in complex with it (Bertolotti et al., 2000; Okamura et al., 2000; Oikawa et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertolotti et al., 2000; Okamura et al., 2000; Oikawa et al., 2009

claim: ERdj4 selectively represses IRE1 activity in vivo.
source: Further molecular insight into the chaperone inhibition mechanism was gained recently by the discovery of ERdj4 as an ER-localised J-domain protein that selectively represses IRE1 activity in vivo and loads BiP onto the IRE1LD, thereby promoting monomerisation in vitro (Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017

claim: ERdj4 loads BiP onto the IRE1LD, thereby promoting monomerisation in vitro.
source: Further molecular insight into the chaperone inhibition mechanism was gained recently by the discovery of ERdj4 as an ER-localised J-domain protein that selectively represses IRE1 activity in vivo and loads BiP onto the IRE1LD, thereby promoting monomerisation in vitro (Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017

claim: Enforced loading of endogenous BiP onto endogenous IRE1α repressed UPR signalling in CHO cells.
source: We report that enforced loading of endogenous BiP onto endogenous IRE1α repressed UPR signalling in CHO cells and deletions in the IRE1α locus that de-repressed the UPR in cells, encode flexible regions of IRE1LD that mediated BiP-induced monomerisation in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Deletions in the IRE1α locus that de-repressed the UPR in cells encode flexible regions of IRE1LD that mediated BiP-induced monomerisation in vitro.
source: We report that enforced loading of endogenous BiP onto endogenous IRE1α repressed UPR signalling in CHO cells and deletions in the IRE1α locus that de-repressed the UPR in cells, encode flexible regions of IRE1LD that mediated BiP-induced monomerisation in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Changes in the hydrogen exchange mass spectrometry profile of IRE1LD induced by ERdj4 and BiP confirmed monomerisation.
source: Changes in the hydrogen exchange mass spectrometry profile of IRE1LD induced by ERdj4 and BiP confirmed monomerisation and were consistent with active destabilisation of the IRE1LD dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Changes in the hydrogen exchange mass spectrometry profile of IRE1LD induced by ERdj4 and BiP were consistent with active destabilisation of the IRE1LD dimer.
source: Changes in the hydrogen exchange mass spectrometry profile of IRE1LD induced by ERdj4 and BiP confirmed monomerisation and were consistent with active destabilisation of the IRE1LD dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Cells expressing the J-IRE1 fusion showed low XBP1::Turquoise reporter levels, indicating repressed IRE1 activity, even under stress.
source: In comparison, cells expressing the J-IRE1 fusion showed low XBP1::Turquoise reporter levels, indicating repressed IRE1 activity, even under stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Repression of IRE1 by J-IRE1 fusion was dependent on the integrity of the J-domain.
source: Repression was dependent on the integrity of the J-domain as ΔIRE1 cells reconstituted with the mutant JQPD-IRE1 acquired nearly wild-type stress responsiveness.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The J-IRE1 protein was still able to respond to the ER stressor SubA.
source: The J-IRE1 protein was not otherwise compromised, as it was still able to respond to the ER stressor SubA, a protease that inactivates BiP by cleaving its interdomain linker (Paton et al., 2006) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Paton et al., 2006

claim: More BiP was recovered in complex with the J-IRE1 chimera compared to the wild-type IRE1.
source: More BiP was recovered in complex with the J-IRE1 chimera compared to the wild-type IRE1 whilst the mutant JQPD-IRE1 fusion associated with a similar amount of BiP as the wild-type (Figure 1C), which is in accordance to their similar phenotype detected by flow cytometry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: BiP recovery in complex with IRE1LD-bio was dependent on the presence of both ERdj4 and ATP in the binding assay.
source: Whilst BiP recovery in complex with IRE1LD-bio was dependent on the presence of both ERdj4 and ATP in the binding assay, complex formation of BiP and J-IRE1LD-bio required only ATP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Complex formation of BiP and J-IRE1LD-bio required only ATP.
source: Whilst BiP recovery in complex with IRE1LD-bio was dependent on the presence of both ERdj4 and ATP in the binding assay, complex formation of BiP and J-IRE1LD-bio required only ATP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: BiP, ERdj4, and ATP were all required to monomerise the IRE1LD homodimer.
source: As previously observed, BiP, ERdj4, and ATP were all required to monomerise the IRE1LD homodimer as reflected in the time-dependent increase in donor fluorescence until a kinetically maintained pseudo steady state was reached (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Heterodimeric FRET pairs containing the J-IRE1LD fusion and IRE1LD were monomerised by BiP in an ATP-dependent manner, but did not require ERdj4 in trans.
source: In contrast, heterodimeric FRET pairs containing the J-IRE1LD fusion and IRE1LD were monomerised by BiP in an ATP-dependent manner, but did not require ERdj4 in trans.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: MPZ-N peptide had no measurable effect on donor fluorescence in the FRET-based assay.
source: When introduced into the FRET-based assay, MPZ-N had no measurable effect on donor fluorescence.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study

claim: Addition of MPZ-N peptide did not affect the peak elution time of IRE1LD in size exclusion chromatography.
source: Addition of MPZ-N peptide (at concentrations exceeding the reported K1/2 max for binding of 16 µM, Karagöz et al., 2017) did not affect the peak elution time of IRE1LD, itself introduced into the assay at 500 nM, near the Kd for IRE1LD dimerisation (Zhou et al., 2006) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B, and citations to Karagöz et al., 2017 and Zhou et al., 2006

claim: The melting temperature (Tm) of disulphide-linked IRE1LD Q105C SS was ~10 °C higher than the Tm of the wild-type protein.
source: Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) revealed that the melting temperature (Tm) of disulphide-linked IRE1LD Q105C SS was ~10 °C higher than the Tm the wild-type protein, a Tm difference that was effaced by reduction of the dimer-stabilising disulphide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Addition of MPZ-N peptide had no effect on the Tm of IRE1LD.
source: A ligand, stabilising the IRE1LD dimer, is predicted to increase the Tm, however, addition of MPZ-N peptide had no effect on the Tm of IRE1LD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, the significance of the lowering of Tm observed at the highest concentrations of peptide remains to be determined).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: The crystallised IRE1LD Q105C SS dimer proved identical in structure to the wild-type protein except for the presence of a C105-C105 trans-protomer disulphide.
source: The crystallised IRE1LD Q105C SS dimer proved identical in structure to the wild-type protein (root-mean squared deviation (RMSD) of 0.46 Å over 227 Cα atoms) except for the presence of a conspicuous density corresponding to a C105-C105 trans-protomer disulphide, thereby locking the proposed binding groove in the 'closed' conformation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and Table 1

claim: Binding of FAM-labelled MPZ-N to IRE1LD was not compromised by the disulphide in IRE1LD Q105C SS.
source: Nonetheless, a fluorescence polarisation binding assay, using FAM-labelled MPZ-N, showed that binding to the IRE1LD was not compromised by the disulphide (Figure 2D), leading us to conclude that MPZ-N does not obligatorily bind within the proposed MHC-like groove of the IRE1LD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: MPZ-N does not obligatorily bind within the proposed MHC-like groove of the IRE1LD.
source: Nonetheless, a fluorescence polarisation binding assay, using FAM-labelled MPZ-N, showed that binding to the IRE1LD was not compromised by the disulphide (Figure 2D), leading us to conclude that MPZ-N does not obligatorily bind within the proposed MHC-like groove of the IRE1LD.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The region encompassing residues 303–378 of IRE1LD is especially flexible.
source: This method identified the region encompassing residues 303–378 as being especially flexible, a conclusion consistent with the observation that though it was present in the constructs used for crystallisation, residues 308–357 were resolved in neither the crystal structures of wild-type IRE1LD (Zhou et al., 2006) (Figure 3A right panel dotted line) nor the disulphide-linked IRE1LD Q105C SS variant here.
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Zhou et al., 2006

claim: Residues 379–444 of IRE1LD covering the tail region are flexible.
source: Similar characteristics apply to residues 379–444, covering the so-called tail region that connects the structured core of the IRE1LD with the transmembrane domain (Figure 3A right panel dotted line and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The tail region of IRE1LD (residues 379–444) overlaps with a region implicated in its basal repression in an overexpression cell-based assay.
source: Moreover, the latter residues overlap with a region of IRE1LD implicated in its basal repression in an overexpression cell-based assay (Oikawa et al., 2007; Oikawa et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oikawa et al., 2007; Oikawa et al., 2009

claim: All the putative deregulating deletions/mutations in IRE1 identified by CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis maintained the frame of the IRE1 coding sequence.
source: As expected, all the putative deregulating deletions/mutations maintained the frame of the IRE1 coding sequence (Figure 3C right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The reconstituted IRE1 deletion alleles (Δloop, Δtail, ΔΔ) de-repressed IRE1 activity, as indicated by elevated basal XBP1s::Turquoise signal.
source: The reconstituted alleles de-repressed IRE1 activity, as indicated by the elevated basal XBP1s::Turquoise signal (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The IRE1 ΔΔ double deletion had the strongest deregulated phenotype under basal conditions.
source: The IRE1 ΔΔ double deletion had the strongest deregulated phenotype under basal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The IRE1 ΔΔ double deletion retained some responsiveness to stress, albeit with a narrowed dynamic range.
source: Like the shorter deletions, the IRE1 ΔΔ double deletion nonetheless retained some responsiveness to stress, albeit with a narrowed dynamic range (Figure 4A, compare untreated to tunicamycin-treated samples).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Significantly less BiP was associated with the IRE1 ΔΔ mutant compared to wild-type IRE1.
source: Despite variation in the total BiP signal intensity in the three independent repeats (Figure 4B, lower panel), paired analysis revealed that significantly less BiP was associated with the IRE1 ΔΔ mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The amount of BiP recovered by glutathione affinity chromatography in association with IRE1LD deletion variants was significantly lower than with wild-type IRE1LD-GST.
source: Compared to the wild-type IRE1LD-GST bait, the amount of BiP recovered by glutathione affinity chromatography in association with the variants was significantly lower in context of the single deletions and even lower in case of the double-deletion IRE1LD ΔΔ-GST (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: BiP association to IRE1LD ΔΔ was reproducibly attenuated compared to wild-type IRE1LD in Bio-Layer Interferometry experiments.
source: Immersing the sensor into a solution containing ERdj4, BiP and ATP gave rise to an association curve, that was reproducibly attenuated when IRE1LD ΔΔ was bound as a ligand compared to the wild-type IRE1LD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, left traces).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: A reproducible defect of BiP association to J-IRE1LD ΔΔ was observed in BLI experiments.
source: Immersing a BLI sensor loaded either with J-IRE1LD or J-IRE1LD ΔΔ into a solution containing BiP and ATP revealed a reproducible defect of BiP association to J-IRE1LD ΔΔ (Figure 5A left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Almost three-fold less BiP was recovered in complex with IRE1LD ∆∆-bio than with IRE1LD-bio in pull-down experiments.
source: Almost three-fold less BiP was recovered in complex with IRE1LD ∆∆-bio than with IRE1LD-bio (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The initial velocity of BiP-mediated monomerisation of the IRE1LD ΔΔ containing heterodimers was considerably slower than monomerisation of wild-type homodimers.
source: The initial velocity of BiP-mediated monomerisation of the IRE1LD ΔΔ containing heterodimers was considerably slower than monomerisation of wild-type homodimers (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: BiP association to monomeric IRE1LD P108A was faster than to the enforced dimeric IRE1LD Q105C SS in BLI experiments.
source: In BLI experiments, BiP association to monomeric IRE1LD P108A was faster than to the enforced dimeric IRE1LD Q105C SS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), raising the concern that both diminished BiP binding to the IRE1LD ΔΔ observed in BLI (Figure 5A) and the slower monomerisation of the IRE1LD ΔΔ containing FRET pair (Figure 5C) might reflect intrinsically enhanced stability of the IRE1LD ΔΔ-containing dimers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: SEC of the purified proteins reported on similar affinities of the wild-type and IRE1LD ΔΔ dimers.
source: However, SEC of the purified proteins performed over a range of protein concentrations reported on similar affinities of the wild-type and IRE1LD ΔΔ dimers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D) yielding K1/2 max values in the same order of magnitude as the KD of dimerisation measured by AUC (Zhou et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D, and citation to Zhou et al., 2006

claim: Monomerisation of IRE1LD affected HX at the dimer interface but also in parts further away.
source: Projecting these areas onto the crystal structure revealed that monomerisation affected HX at the dimer interface but also in parts further away (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: IRE1LD monomerisation induced structural rearrangements across the protein.
source: IRE1LD monomerisation thus induced structural rearrangements across the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on HX-MS data shown in Figure 6

claim: A similar deprotection signature to that observed in monomeric IRE1LD mutants was observed when IRE1LD was incubated with BiP and ERdj4 in presence of ATP.
source: A similar deprotection signature, affecting most of the peptic peptides that are exposed upon monomerisation, was observed when IRE1LD was incubated with BiP and ERdj4 in presence of ATP (Figure 6C upper row, box 1: residues 77–128 and box 2: residues 280–302).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: IRE1LD ΔΔ exhibited delayed monomerisation in presence of BiP, ERdj4 and ATP as assessed by HX-MS.
source: IRE1LD ΔΔ exhibited delayed monomerisation in presence of BiP, ERdj4 and ATP: IRE1LD ΔΔ's signature of monomerisation was absent after 30 s incubation in D2O (Figure 6C lower row) and was faint even after an exchange reaction of 300 s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C lower row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: In the absence of BiP, ERdj4 and ATP the difference plot comparing deuteron incorporation into IRE1LD and IRE1LD ΔΔ was negligible.
source: In the absence of BiP, ERdj4 and ATP the difference plot comparing deuteron incorporation into IRE1LD and IRE1LD ΔΔ was negligible (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) providing independent confirmation of the SEC measurements pointing to similar stability of the wild-type and IRE1LD ΔΔ mutant dimer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: Some peptic peptides from IRE1LD exhibited clear bimodal isotope distribution, a signature for the EX1 exchange regime.
source: Close inspection of the HX-MS data revealed that some of the peptides (e.g. peptides 636.3802+ and 655.273+ corresponding to residues 96–106 and 297–302, respectively) exhibited clear bimodal isotope distribution. This characteristic is a signature for the EX1 exchange regime, indicative of the presence of two discrete subpopulations of molecules: a more folded and therefore low exchanging subpopulation and a more open, high exchanging subpopulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: The low exchanging subpopulation of IRE1LD was largely protected from HX, whereas the high exchanging subpopulation had almost all amide protons exchanged for deuterons.
source: Comparison with the unexchanged and the 100% control samples revealed that the low exchanging subpopulation was largely protected from HX, whereas the high exchanging subpopulation had almost all amide protons exchanged for deuterons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: The low exchanging subpopulation of IRE1LD converted into the high exchanging subpopulation with time.
source: Moreover, the low exchanging subpopulation converted into the high exchanging subpopulation with time (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, compare 30 and 300 s incubation in D2O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: The degree of conversion into the high exchanging subpopulation was more pronounced for the IRE1LD P108A monomeric mutant than for wild-type IRE1LD.
source: Interestingly, the degree of conversion into the high exchanging subpopulation was more pronounced for the IRE1LD P108A monomeric mutant than for wild-type IRE1LD and essentially complete after 300 s (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: The transition from the low exchanging subpopulation to the high exchanging subpopulation was a feature of the monomeric state of IRE1LD.
source: Hence, these data suggest that the conversion from the low exchanging subpopulation to the high exchanging subpopulation was a feature of the monomeric state.
evidence: This is an inference based on HX-MS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: An accelerated time-dependent increase in the proportion of monomeric IRE1LD was observed in the BiP-treated sample, indicating an increase in ktrans.
source: Nevertheless, an accelerated time-dependent increase in the proportion of monomeric IRE1LD was observed in the BiP-treated sample, indicating an increase in ktrans (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: BiP-induced IRE1LD monomerisation has a component arising from active destabilisation of the dimer.
source: Therefore, these findings imply that BiP-induced IRE1LD monomerisation has a component arising from active destabilisation of the dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on HX-MS data shown in Figure 7

claim: Directing endogenous BiP to bind endogenous IRE1LD as a substrate attenuates signalling in cells.
source: Here, we provide much needed further support for the chaperone repression model by demonstrating that directing endogenous BiP to bind endogenous IRE1LD as a substrate also attenuates signalling in cells, thus revealing BiP's potential as a direct IRE1 repressor in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Regions of IRE1LD that impart a repressed state in vivo proved important for ATP and co-chaperone-dependent BiP-mediated conversion of active-state IRE1LD dimers to inactive-state monomers in vitro.
source: A structure-based targeted approach identified regions of IRE1LD that impart a repressed state in vivo. The same regions proved important for ATP and co-chaperone-dependent BiP-mediated conversion of active-state IRE1LD dimers to inactive-state monomers in vitro and their presence accelerated the formation of an ATP and co-chaperone-dependent complex with BiP in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The presence of flexible regions in IRE1LD accelerated the formation of an ATP and co-chaperone-dependent complex with BiP in vitro.
source: A structure-based targeted approach identified regions of IRE1LD that impart a repressed state in vivo. The same regions proved important for ATP and co-chaperone-dependent BiP-mediated conversion of active-state IRE1LD dimers to inactive-state monomers in vitro and their presence accelerated the formation of an ATP and co-chaperone-dependent complex with BiP in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A disulphide crystallographically proven to lie across the MHC-like groove of IRE1LD had no effect on the binding of MPZ-N to IRE1LD.
source: Our findings do not support the notion that this peptide specifically engages the MHC-like groove traversing the dimer interface, as a disulphide, crystallographically proven to lie across this groove, thereby locking the helices in a 'closed' conformation, had no effect on the binding of MPZ-N to IRE1LD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: MPZ-N binding to IRE1LD did not stabilise it thermodynamically.
source: Furthermore, MPZ-N binding to IRE1LD did not stabilise it thermodynamically, whereas the aforementioned disulphide, which mimics the proposed dimer-stabilising effect of a bound peptide, increased the melting temperature IRE1LD by 10 °C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: MPZ-N did not promote a shift in the monomer-dimer equilibrium of IRE1LD as assessed by SEC.
source: Nor did MPZ-N promote a shift in the monomer-dimer equilibrium of IRE1LD as assessed by SEC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: BiP, as an Hsp70 chaperone, typically interacts with unfolded or flexible regions in its client proteins.
source: BiP, as an Hsp70 chaperone, typically interacts with unfolded or flexible regions in its client proteins (Rüdiger et al., 1997) and we held that this might also be the case for its interaction with the IRE1LD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rüdiger et al., 1997

claim: Considerable redundancy is built into the process of BiP-mediated IRE1 repression.
source: Considerable redundancy seems built into the process, as the deregulated IRE1∆∆ allele retained a measure of stress responsiveness in cells and the IRE1LD ∆∆ dimer was still slowly undone in a BiP-dependent process in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: In both yeast and human, IRE1 deletion of the tail region partially deregulated IRE1, whilst retaining partial responsiveness to ER stress.
source: Such redundancy has been observed previously: in both yeast and human, IRE1 deletion of the tail region connecting the structured core of IRE1LD to the transmembrane domain partially deregulated IRE1, whilst retaining partial responsiveness to ER stress (Oikawa et al., 2007; Oikawa et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oikawa et al., 2007; Oikawa et al., 2009

claim: Redundancy in the structural features of the IRE1LD dimer that render it a substrate for BiP-dependent disassembly and the non-equilibrium kinetic nature for BiP's action could serve as the basis for a smoothly graded response to variation in the levels of ER stress.
source: Redundancy in the structural features of the IRE1LD dimer that render it a substrate for BiP-dependent disassembly and the non-equilibrium kinetic nature for BiP's action could serve as the basis for a smoothly graded response to variation in the levels of ER stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings
